newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egyptian central bank to tighten bank supervision.
newsitem.headline: Egyptian central bank to tighten bank supervision.

text.p: The Central Bank of Egypt will tighten up its supervision of banks by applying new accounting and disclosure rules from July, a senior bank official said.
Faika el-Rifaie, the central bank sub-governor for research, was speaking at a seminar in Alexandria and was quoted on Monday in the government newspaper al-Ahram.
"Starting July 1 Egyptian banks will be subject to new accounting rules under which they must increase the element of disclosure and publish statistics on their activity," she said.

"This is in the context of increasing transparency, which is an objective of the central bank... The new rules will make it possible to provide better supervision of the banks operating in Egypt," she added.
The newspaper gave no other details of the changes and Rifaie was not available in her office on Monday.
Under the present system most Egyptian bank balance sheets give no indication of the quality of loans or the amount of non-performing loans they hold.
Some economists say that in the case of the big public-sector banks the non-performing loans could amount to between 35 and 40 percent of total loans.
The quality of bank supervision has been in the spotlight this year as the state prepares to privatise one of the four public-sector banks. It has not said which one.
Prime Minister Kamal Ganzouri, in a speech on Sunday, assured parliament that the banking sector was in good shape.

But at an economic conference in February Rifaie said that three banks in Egypt had failed to meet the capital adequacy ratio set by the Basle Accord, six years after the Central Bank told them to do so by the end of 1993.
She was responding to a damning review of bank supervision by an academic and consultant to the prime minister's office.

The academic, Mahmoud Mohiedin of Cairo University, said that rather than let any Egyptian-based bank fail, the Central Bank preferred to relax prudential measures, for example by waiving its own reserve and liquidity requirements. -- Jonathan Wright Cairo Newsroom +20 2 578 3290/1
